tomorrow/fr.text: Pour jeudi 22 octobre 2026 : l’ordinaire est estimée à 189,4 ¢/L à Montréal et à 173,1 ¢/L à Toronto. Le prix de l’essence de demain n’est publié nulle part officiellement : cette page l’estime à partir de ce qui l’est. Pour chaque ville, elle prend le dernier chiffre officiel (relevé quotidien de la Régie de l’énergie au Québec, relevé hebdomadaire de l’Ontario, prix maximal d’un régulateur de l’Atlantique ou moyenne mensuelle de Statistique Canada), ajoute la variation du prix de gros publiée depuis, multipliée par un plus le taux de taxe de vente, puis tout changement de taxe déjà daté pour demain. Pour le 22 octobre 2026, cela donne 189,4 ¢/L pour l’ordinaire à Montréal, où le relevé de la Régie du 21 octobre 2026 est déjà celui du jour, et 173,1 ¢/L à Toronto, contre 176,7 ¢/L au relevé du 19 octobre 2026. Parmi les villes qui ont un chiffre quotidien ou hebdomadaire, 5 sont orientées à la baisse, 0 à la hausse et 8 sans changement. Rejouée sur 140 semaines à Toronto, la méthode s’est trompée de 2,4 ¢/L en moyenne, contre 3,8 ¢/L en répétant le dernier prix. De quoi est faite l’estimation Trois choses peuvent déplacer un prix à la pompe entre un chiffre officiel et demain : le prix de l’essence sur le marché de gros, les marges des grossistes et des détaillants, et les taxes. Les marges ne sont pas publiées : la méthode suppose qu’elles restent là où elles étaient au dernier relevé. Le prix de gros et les taxes sont publiés, et la méthode utilise les deux. Pour le prix de gros, le gouvernement de l’Ontario publie chaque jour le prix à la rampe de Toronto, Thunder Bay et Edmonton, mais avec environ une semaine de retard. C’est assez pour mettre à jour une moyenne mensuelle de Statistique Canada, rarement pour les jours qui suivent un relevé du lundi. Pour ces jours-là, la méthode lit la Régie de l’énergie du Québec, dont le relevé des prix affichés dans la région de Montréal paraît chaque matin de semaine. Une fois retirées la TPS, la TVQ, la taxe québécoise sur les carburants, la taxe de l’ARTM et l’accise fédérale, le reste suit le marché de gros qui approvisionne l’Ontario, le Québec et l’Atlantique. La variation de ce chiffre avant taxes depuis le dernier relevé, multipliée par un plus la taxe de vente locale, forme la partie « marché » de l’estimation. Les taxes sont plus simples : elles changent à des dates fixées par la loi. L’accise fédérale, le taux trimestriel de la taxe albertaine et la suspension de la taxe à l’Île-du-Prince-Édouard sont saisis avec leurs dates : l’estimation du jour où un changement entre en vigueur l’inclut au cent près. Trois sortes de point de départ Au Québec, le point de départ est le relevé du matin de la Régie, déjà un chiffre du jour : l’estimation du lendemain ne peut y ajouter qu’un changement de taxe, et Montréal se trouve à 189,4 ¢/L. En Ontario, c’est le relevé du lundi : celui d’Ottawa était de 170,8 ¢/L le 19 octobre 2026. Dans l’Atlantique, c’est un maximum légal qui change à des jours connus : le plafond de 193,1 ¢/L d’Halifax s’applique depuis le 16 octobre 2026 et reste en place jusqu’à la révision du vendredi, sauf intervention de la régie en semaine. Dans l’Ouest, faute de source ouverte quotidienne ou hebdomadaire, le point de départ est la moyenne de Statistique Canada de septembre 2026, ramenée à aujourd’hui par le prix de gros d’Edmonton. Ce qu’a valu l’estimation La méthode est rejouée sur le passé pour chaque ville et chaque carburant : à partir de chaque relevé, elle estime le suivant avec ce qui était publié la veille seulement, semaine de retard des prix de gros comprise, puis compare au chiffre réellement publié. Chaque page de ville affiche l’écart moyen à côté de celui d’une prévision « sans changement ». Quand la méthode ne fait pas mieux, comme pour le diesel, la page le dit. Le tableau complet est sur la page Méthode . L’écart est mesuré sur des moyennes officielles. Une station donnée peut se situer plusieurs cents au-dessus ou en dessous de la moyenne de sa ville et changer son affichage à toute heure : l’estimation dit où va la moyenne, pas ce qu’une station affichera. S’en servir pour choisir le jour du plein Comparez l’écart entre le chiffre du jour et l’estimation de demain avec l’écart habituel de la méthode dans votre ville. Un écart nettement plus grand traduit un mouvement du marché que les sources montrent déjà ; un écart plus petit reste dans le bruit, et les deux jours se valent. Sur un plein de 55 litres, chaque cent vaut 55 cents : à Toronto, l’écart entre le dernier relevé et l’estimation de demain représente 1,98 $. Pour la suite, que personne ne peut connaître, voyez ce qui est déjà prévu dans la page sur les taxes de l’essence . À quelle heure le prix de l’essence change-t-il pour le lendemain ? Il n’y a pas d’heure unique. Bien des stations changent leur prix pendant la nuit, après que leur fournisseur a mis à jour le prix de gros à la rampe, et les régulateurs de l’Atlantique font entrer leurs nouveaux maximums en vigueur à 0 h 01, d’habitude le vendredi. L’estimation de cette page est refaite chaque jour avec les sources publiées le matin : elle décrit la journée de demain, pas une heure précise. Pourquoi l’estimation de demain est-elle parfois égale au prix du jour ? Quand aucun prix de gros plus récent que le dernier relevé officiel n’a été publié, ou quand un prix maximal réglementé n’est pas refixé demain, rien ne permet de déplacer le chiffre. La page montre alors le prix officiel inchangé et dit pourquoi, au lieu d’inventer une hausse ou une baisse qu’aucune source n’appuie. Peut-on se fier à une prévision du prix de l’essence à un jour ? C’est une estimation informée dont l’écart est connu. Pour l’essence ordinaire à Toronto, la méthode publiée s’est trompée de 2,4 ¢/L en moyenne sur le relevé suivant, 37 % de moins qu’une prévision « sans changement ». Pour le diesel, elle ne fait pas mieux, ce que chaque page de ville affiche. Aucune méthode ne sait ce qu’une station affichera. Le retour de la taxe d’accise fédérale est-il compté dans l’estimation ? Oui. Le calendrier de la taxe d’accise fédérale est saisi avec ses dates : zéro jusqu’au 31 janvier 2027, demi-taux le 1er février 2027 et plein taux le 1er avril 2027 selon l’avant-projet de loi. La veille de chaque date, l’estimation du lendemain ajoute le changement, taxe de vente comprise, dans toutes les provinces.

tomorrow/en.text: For Thursday, October 22, 2026: regular is estimated at 173.1¢/L in Toronto and 189.4¢/L in Montreal. Tomorrow's gas price is not published anywhere officially, so this page estimates it from what is. For each city it takes the latest official figure (a weekly Ontario survey, the Régie de l'énergie's daily Quebec survey, an Atlantic regulator's maximum, or a Statistics Canada monthly average), adds the change in wholesale prices published since, multiplied by one plus the sales tax rate, and adds any tax change already dated for tomorrow. For October 22, 2026, that gives 173.1¢/L for regular in Toronto, against 176.7¢/L at the October 19, 2026 survey, and 156.1¢/L in Calgary, where the September average still included the Alberta fuel tax suspended on October 1. Among cities with a daily or weekly figure, 5 point down, 0 up and 8 unchanged. Replayed over 140 past weeks in Toronto, the method missed by 2.4¢/L on average, against 3.8¢/L for repeating the last price. What the estimate is made of Three things can move a pump price between one official figure and tomorrow: the price of gasoline on the wholesale market, the margins of wholesalers and retailers, and taxes. Margins are not published, so the method assumes they stay where they were at the last survey. Wholesale prices and taxes are published, and the method uses both. For wholesale prices, the Government of Ontario publishes daily rack prices for Toronto, Thunder Bay and Edmonton, but about a week late. That is enough to bring a Statistics Canada monthly average up to date, but it rarely says anything about the days after a Monday survey. For those days the method reads the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, whose survey of posted prices in the Montréal region comes out every weekday morning. Once GST, QST, the Quebec fuel tax, the transit levy and the federal excise tax are taken out, the rest moves with the wholesale market that supplies Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. The change in that pre-tax figure since the last survey, times one plus the local sales tax, is the market part of the estimate. Taxes are simpler: they change on dates set by law. The federal excise tax, Alberta's quarterly fuel tax rate and Prince Edward Island's suspension are all entered with their dates, so the estimate for the day a change takes effect includes it to the cent. Three kinds of starting point In Ontario the starting point is the Monday survey: Ottawa's was 170.8¢/L on October 19, 2026. In Quebec it is the morning survey of the Régie, already a figure for today, so the estimate for tomorrow can only add a tax change; Montreal stands at 189.4¢/L. In the Atlantic provinces it is a legal maximum that changes on known days: Halifax's ceiling of 193.1¢/L has applied since October 16, 2026 and stays until the next Friday reset unless the Nova Scotia Energy Board intervenes mid-week. In the West, where no open daily or weekly source exists, the starting point is the Statistics Canada average for September 2026, brought forward by Edmonton rack prices. How good the estimate has been The method is replayed on the past for every city and fuel: from each survey it estimates the next one using only what had been published the day before, including the week of delay on rack prices, then compares with what was actually published. Each city page prints the average miss next to the miss of a "no change" guess. When the method does not beat that guess, as for diesel, the page says so. The complete table is on the method page . The error is measured on official averages. A single station can sit several cents away from the average of its city, in either direction, and can change its sign at any hour: the estimate tells you where the average is heading, not what one forecourt will post. Using it to decide when to fill up Compare the gap between today's figure and tomorrow's estimate with the method's usual miss for your city. A gap well above that miss is a market move the sources already show; a gap below it is within the noise, and the two days are effectively the same. On a 55-litre fill-up, each cent is 55 cents: in Toronto, the gap between the last survey and tomorrow's estimate is worth $1.98. For the price trend beyond tomorrow, which no source can tell, see what is already scheduled on the gas price forecast page . At what time do gas prices change for tomorrow? There is no single time. Many stations reprice overnight after their supplier updates the wholesale rack price, and Atlantic regulators make new maximums take effect at 12:01 a.m., usually on Fridays. The estimate on this page is rebuilt every day from the sources published that morning, so it describes tomorrow as a whole rather than a given hour. Why does the estimate sometimes equal today’s price? When no wholesale price newer than the latest official survey has been published, or when a regulated maximum is not reset tomorrow, there is nothing to move the figure with. The page then shows the official price unchanged and says why, rather than inventing a rise or a fall that no source supports. Can I trust a one-day gas price prediction? Treat it as a well-informed estimate with a known error. For Toronto regular gasoline, the published method has missed the next weekly survey by 2.4¢/L on average, 37% less than guessing no change. For diesel it is no better than no change, which each city page shows. No method knows what one station will post. Does the estimate include the return of the federal excise tax? Yes. The schedule of the federal excise tax is entered with its dates: zero until January 31, 2027, half rate on February 1, 2027 and full rate on April 1, 2027 under the draft legislation. On the eve of each date, the estimate for the next day adds the change, sales tax included, in every province.

forecast/en.text: If the draft schedule is enacted, the federal excise tax will add 11.3¢/L to a litre of regular in Ontario from April 1, 2027. Nobody can forecast the market price of gasoline months ahead: it follows crude oil, refinery margins and the exchange rate, none of which is known in advance. What can be forecast are the tax changes that already have a date. The largest is the federal excise tax, suspended since April 20, 2026: under Finance Canada's draft legislation it returns at 5¢/L on February 1, 2027 and at 10¢/L on April 1, 2027, which, sales tax included, adds 11.3¢/L to a litre of regular in Ontario. Prince Edward Island's 8.47¢/L gasoline tax is suspended until January 31, 2027, and Alberta's 13¢/L tax is not collected until at least December 31, 2026; from 2027 it depends each quarter on the price of WTI oil. For context, the Statistics Canada average for September 2026 was 184.3¢/L, 27.8% above September 2025. The calendar of known changes Four dates are written into law or into published drafts. On January 1, 2027 at the earliest, Alberta may start collecting its fuel tax again, at a rate set by the oil price. On February 1, 2027, Prince Edward Island's suspension ends and the federal excise comes back at half rate. On April 1, 2027, the excise returns in full. Each step is entered in the site's tax tables with its date, so the estimate for the day it takes effect already includes it. The table shows what the excise return means in each province, sales tax included. The provinces with a harmonized sales tax see a little more than the 10 cents, because HST is charged on the excise itself. These steps come from draft legislation: Parliament can still change the dates or the rates. When the law is enacted or amended, the table and the calculators follow the official text on the next daily update. The last twelve weeks To give a sense of scale, the weekly Ontario survey for Toronto ranged from 162.3¢/L (August 10, 2026) to 186.9¢/L (October 5, 2026) over the last twelve weeks published, without any tax change in that period. The market alone moved the price by 24.6¢/L, more than the full return of the excise. Planning a budget on the tax calendar alone would therefore miss most of the variation. Prince Edward Island, a double step in February February 1, 2027 is the day two changes meet on the Island. The provincial gasoline tax of 8.47¢/L, suspended since September 26, 2026, comes back the same day the federal excise returns at half rate. With HST at 15% on top, a litre of regular would carry 15.5¢/L more than in January, before any market move. This site follows the Island only through its tax tables for now: no open city average for Charlottetown is published, so there is no price to carry forward, only the tax part, which the calculator gives exactly. Diesel follows the same calendar with smaller federal steps: 2¢/L in February and 4¢/L in April. The calculator above switches to diesel with the fuel choice. Alberta, a moving rate Alberta's relief program ties the provincial fuel tax to WTI oil: the higher the crude price, the lower the tax, with four possible rates and a cap of 9 cents of increase per quarter. The September Statistics Canada average for Calgary, 167.3¢/L, still included the tax; the estimate for tomorrow removes it, which is why the Calgary page shows a figure well below the monthly average. The rate for the first quarter of 2027 is not known yet, and this site will not guess it. Why no market forecast Estimating tomorrow is possible because the wholesale prices of the past few days are already published and pass to the pump with a short delay. Beyond a few days, the method has nothing to work with: futures prices for gasoline exist, but they are not open data, and they are a poor guide to the price at a given station months away. So this page gives what is certain, the dated tax changes, and leaves the market part blank. For the next day, with its measured error, see the gas price tomorrow page . Will gas prices go up in Canada in 2027? Taxes will, on known dates, if the draft legislation is enacted: the federal excise returns in two steps, in February and April 2027, worth 11.3¢/L a litre in Ontario with HST. Whether the pump price rises overall depends on the market, which may move by more than that in either direction over the same months. Is there an official gas price forecast for Canada? No federal or provincial agency publishes a forecast of pump prices by city. Statistics Canada, the provinces and the regulators publish what prices were, not what they will be. Any figure presented as a month-ahead city forecast is a model, and this site only estimates the next day, with its past error printed next to it. When does the Alberta fuel tax come back? Not before January 1, 2027. Under the Fuel Tax Relief Program the 13¢/L tax is not collected from October 1 to at least December 31, 2026. After that, the rate is set each quarter at 0, 4.5, 9 or 13 cents depending on the WTI oil price, and it can rise by 9 cents at most from one quarter to the next.

diesel/en.text: Diesel was 261.5¢/L in Toronto at the October 19, 2026 survey, 84.8¢/L more than regular. Diesel costs more than regular gasoline in every city this site follows: on average 84.3¢/L more per litre today, from 230.4¢/L in Edmonton to 298.7¢/L in Laval. The gap comes from the wholesale market, not from taxes: at the Toronto rack, the last published price was 216.3¢/L for diesel against 137.3¢/L for gasoline (October 14, 2026). Official diesel figures come from the same sources as gasoline: the weekly Ontario survey, the maximum prices of the Atlantic regulators and the monthly averages of Statistics Canada; the Régie de l'énergie's daily survey covers regular gasoline only. For the same reason, the estimate for tomorrow moves diesel only with rack prices, which Ontario publishes a week late, and on most days it equals the last official figure. Across Canada, Statistics Canada's monthly average for diesel is not used here; each city has its own figure and date. Diesel, city by city The table ranks the cities by diesel price and shows the gap with regular gasoline on the same basis. Cities that only have a monthly Statistics Canada average show the estimate for tomorrow, labelled as such; the others show their latest official figure, with its date. Two things stand out. First, the gap with gasoline is wide everywhere, which points to the wholesale market rather than to any provincial policy. Second, taxes shift the picture only a little: per-litre diesel taxes are higher than gasoline taxes in Quebec, New Brunswick and Newfoundland and Labrador, equal in Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and the 3-cent ARTM levy of the Montréal region applies to gasoline only. Why the estimate for diesel rarely moves For gasoline, this site carries the last official figure forward with a daily signal: the Régie de l'énergie's morning survey in the Montréal region, once its taxes are removed. No such daily survey is published for diesel. The only market data are the daily rack prices that Ontario publishes for Toronto, Thunder Bay and Edmonton, about a week after the fact. When those prices are newer than the last survey, which happens with monthly averages, the estimate moves; with a weekly survey, it usually does not. The past error is printed regardless. For Toronto diesel, the method missed the next weekly survey by 4.5¢/L on average over 140 weeks, the same as repeating the last price. Saying so is more useful than a confident number nobody can check. Diesel taxes The federal excise tax on diesel is 4 cents a litre, suspended since April 20, 2026 like the 10-cent tax on gasoline. Under Finance Canada's draft legislation it returns at 2 cents on February 1, 2027 and at 4 cents on April 1, 2027. Provincial rates on diesel are 9 cents in Ontario, 20.2 in Quebec, 15 in British Columbia outside the transit regions, 15 in Saskatchewan, 12.5 in Manitoba, 15.4 in Nova Scotia, 15.45 in New Brunswick and 9.5 in Newfoundland and Labrador. Alberta's 13-cent tax, on diesel as on gasoline, has not been collected since October 1, 2026. Sales tax applies on top, and businesses registered for GST or HST recover it as an input tax credit. The cost of running on diesel Diesel engines use fewer litres for the same distance, which offsets part of the higher price. Natural Resources Canada's 2026 fuel consumption ratings give a median of 10.3 L/100 km for standard diesel pickups and 12.9 for gasoline ones. Whether the diesel version costs less to run depends on the price gap in your city, which you can test with the budget calculator on the city ranking page or the fill-up calculator below. Fleet and farm use For a business, the useful price is the one before sales tax, since GST or HST paid on fuel is recovered as an input tax credit. The tax calculator above separates that line, so the net cost per litre can be read directly. Diesel used off the road, on farms or in fishing boats, is taxed under separate provincial rules that this site does not model: the figures here are road diesel at the pump. For a heavy vehicle, the monthly budget tool lets you enter the litres you buy and see how a one-cent move in the price changes the bill. Atlantic regulators set the diesel maximum along with the gasoline one: in Halifax and Moncton the ceiling is reset on Fridays, in St. John's every day for now. A ceiling is not an average: stations may sell below it. Why is diesel more expensive than gasoline in Canada in 2026? Because diesel is priced on its own wholesale market, the market for distillates that also supplies trucking, farming and heating oil. At the last published Toronto rack prices, diesel was 79.0¢/L above gasoline before any tax. Per-litre taxes on diesel are similar to those on gasoline, and the federal excise is lower, so taxes do not explain the gap. Is there a forecast for diesel prices tomorrow? Each city page gives one, built with the same rule as for gasoline. But no open daily diesel survey exists, so the estimate moves only when Ontario publishes rack prices newer than the last survey, about a week late. On most days it therefore equals the last official figure, and its past error is the same as that of a “no change” guess, which the page says. How much does a diesel pickup cost to run per year? Natural Resources Canada’s 2026 ratings give a median of 10.3 L/100 km for standard diesel pickups, against 12.9 for gasoline ones. Over 20,000 km at Toronto’s diesel price that is about $5,387 a year, against $4,466 for a gasoline pickup at the regular price.

taxes/fr.text: À Montréal, 24,7 % d’un litre d’ordinaire est fait de taxes ; à Toronto, 16,6 % ; à Calgary, 4,8 %. Un litre d’essence au Canada porte jusqu’à trois couches de taxes en plus du coût du produit : une taxe provinciale en cents par litre, parfois une taxe régionale pour le transport collectif, et une taxe de vente calculée sur le tout, ces deux premières comprises. La taxe d’accise fédérale de 10 cents sur l’essence et de 4 cents sur le diesel, quatrième couche, est suspendue depuis le 20 avril 2026, et la redevance carbone fédérale des consommateurs est à zéro depuis le 1er avril 2025. Aux prix du jour, il reste ainsi 46,9 ¢/L de taxes dans un litre à Montréal (19,2 cents de taxe québécoise, 3 cents pour l’ARTM, puis la TPS et la TVQ), 29,3 ¢/L à Toronto (9 cents de taxe ontarienne et TVH de 13 %), 37,1 ¢/L à Vancouver (27 cents de taxe provinciale et de TransLink plus la TPS) et 7,4 ¢/L à Calgary, où l’Alberta ne perçoit plus sa taxe de 13 cents depuis le 1er octobre 2026. Selon l’avant-projet de loi de Finances Canada, l’accise revient à demi-taux le 1er février 2027 et en entier le 1er avril 2027. Quatre couches, dans l’ordre L’ordre compte, parce que la taxe de vente vient en dernier, sur une base qui comprend déjà les autres taxes. On part du prix du produit raffiné livré à la station, avec les marges du grossiste et du détaillant. On ajoute la taxe provinciale sur les carburants, un montant fixe par litre qui ne bouge pas avec le prix. On ajoute la taxe régionale quand elle existe : 3 cents sur l’essence dans le territoire de l’Autorité régionale de transport métropolitain, les parts TransLink et BC Transit de la taxe britanno-colombienne autour de Vancouver et de Victoria. On ajoute l’accise fédérale, à zéro depuis le 20 avril 2026. Puis on applique la taxe de vente de la province : TPS de 5 % dans l’Ouest, TVH de 13 % en Ontario, de 14 % en Nouvelle-Écosse depuis le 1er avril 2025, de 15 % au Nouveau-Brunswick, à Terre-Neuve-et-Labrador et à l’Île-du-Prince-Édouard, et TPS de 5 % plus TVQ de 9,975 % au Québec. Le diesel a son propre barème Dans la plupart des provinces, le diesel porte des taux au litre différents de ceux de l’essence : 15,45 cents contre 10,87 au Nouveau-Brunswick, 9,5 contre 7,5 à Terre-Neuve-et-Labrador, 20,2 contre 19,2 au Québec, où la taxe de 3 cents de l’ARTM ne vise que l’essence. L’accise fédérale sur le diesel est de 4 cents, pas de 10 : son retour en 2027 pèsera moins sur un camion que sur une voiture. Comme le diesel se vend nettement plus cher que l’essence à la fin de 2026, la taxe de vente sur un litre de diesel est plus élevée en cents, même là où la taxe fixe est identique, et la part totale des taxes dans le prix est plus faible. Pour les entreprises inscrites, la TPS, la TVH et la TVQ payées sur le carburant se récupèrent en crédits de taxe sur les intrants, ce qui n’est pas le cas des taxes au litre. Ce que cela donne dans quelques villes Comme les taxes au litre sont fixes et la taxe de vente proportionnelle, la part des taxes dans un litre baisse quand le prix monte. C’est pourquoi deux villes qui ont la même taxe provinciale peuvent afficher le même jour des parts un peu différentes. Le tableau prend le prix du jour là où existe un chiffre officiel quotidien ou hebdomadaire, et l’estimation du lendemain là où le dernier chiffre est une moyenne mensuelle. Les taxes qui ont changé en 2025 et 2026 Plusieurs couches ont bougé récemment : les décompositions vieilles d’un an qu’on trouve ailleurs sont fausses. La redevance carbone fédérale des consommateurs, qui avait atteint 17,61 cents le litre d’essence, est passée à zéro le 1er avril 2025, et la Colombie-Britannique a supprimé sa propre taxe carbone le même jour. La TVH de la Nouvelle-Écosse est passée de 15 % à 14 % le 1er avril 2025. L’Ontario a rendu permanente sa taxe de 9 cents le 1er juillet 2025. Le congé de taxe du Manitoba en 2024 a pris fin le 1er janvier 2025. L’accise fédérale a été suspendue le 20 avril 2026. L’Île-du-Prince-Édouard a suspendu sa taxe provinciale du 26 septembre 2026 au 31 janvier 2027, et l’Alberta a mis en pause sa taxe de 13 cents du 1er octobre au 31 décembre 2026 au moins. Au Québec, la taxe sur les carburants est restée à 19,2 cents. Ce qui est déjà prévu Deux changements sont déjà datés. Selon l’avant-projet de loi de Finances Canada de septembre 2026, l’accise revient à 5 cents sur l’essence et 2 cents sur le diesel du 1er février au 31 mars 2027, puis à ses 10 et 4 cents le 1er avril 2027. En Alberta, le taux trimestriel à partir du 1er janvier 2027 sera de 0, 4,5, 9 ou 13 cents selon le prix moyen du pétrole WTI, sans pouvoir monter de plus de 9 cents en un trimestre. L’estimation de ce site ajoute un changement daté le jour où il entre en vigueur, taxe de vente comprise. La TPS et la TVQ s’appliquent-elles sur la taxe sur l’essence ? Oui. La TPS et la TVQ au Québec, la TVH ou la TPS ailleurs, sont calculées sur le prix à la pompe qui comprend déjà la taxe provinciale sur les carburants, la taxe régionale éventuelle et l’accise fédérale quand elle s’applique. Une hausse de taxe de 10 cents le litre déplace donc le prix d’un peu moins de 11,5 cents au Québec et de 11,3 cents en Ontario. Quelle province taxe le plus l’essence au litre ? Parmi les villes suivies par ce site, le Grand Vancouver porte la taxe au litre la plus forte, 27 cents dont 18,5 cents pour TransLink, suivi de la région de Montréal, où la taxe québécoise de 19,2 cents et la taxe de 3 cents de l’ARTM font 22,2 cents. L’Alberta est la plus basse à la fin de 2026, avec sa taxe provinciale ramenée à zéro. Combien le retour de l’accise ajoutera-t-il au Québec ? Avec la TPS et la TVQ, le retour complet des 10 cents le 1er avril 2027 ajoute 11,50 ¢/L par litre au Québec, environ 6,32 $ sur un plein de 55 litres. Février et mars 2027 portent la moitié de ces montants si l’avant-projet de loi est adopté sans changement. Le marché du carbone du Québec ajoute-t-il une taxe à la pompe ? Aucune ligne distincte n’apparaît. Le coût du système de plafonnement et d’échange de droits d’émission (SPEDE), que les distributeurs doivent couvrir, est déjà compris dans le prix de gros, comme le précise la Régie de l’énergie dans sa publication des prix à la rampe de Montréal. Il se trouve donc dans la part « produit » de la décomposition, pas dans les taxes.

taxes/en.text: In Toronto 16.6% of a litre of regular is tax, in Montreal 24.7%, in Calgary 4.8%. A litre of gasoline in Canada carries up to three layers of tax on top of its product cost: a provincial fuel tax in cents per litre, sometimes a regional transit levy, and a sales tax applied to everything including the first two. The federal excise tax of 10 cents on gasoline and 4 cents on diesel, the fourth layer, has been suspended since April 20, 2026, and the federal consumer carbon charge has been zero since April 1, 2025. At today's prices that leaves 29.3¢/L of tax in a Toronto litre (Ontario's 9 cents plus 13% HST), 46.9¢/L in Montreal (19.2 cents of Quebec fuel tax, 3 cents for the ARTM, then GST and QST), 37.1¢/L in Vancouver (27 cents of provincial and TransLink tax plus GST) and 7.4¢/L in Calgary, where Alberta stopped collecting its 13-cent tax on October 1, 2026. Under Finance Canada's draft legislation, the excise returns at half rate on February 1, 2027 and in full on April 1, 2027. Four layers, in order The order matters because the sales tax is charged last, on a base that already includes the other taxes. Start from the price of the refined product delivered to the station, with the wholesaler's and retailer's margins. Add the provincial fuel tax, a fixed amount per litre that does not move with the price. Add the regional levy where one exists: 3 cents on gasoline in the Montreal metropolitan transit territory, the TransLink and BC Transit shares of the British Columbia motor fuel tax around Vancouver and Victoria. Add the federal excise tax, zero since April 20, 2026. Then apply the sales tax of the province: 5% GST in the West, 13% HST in Ontario, 14% in Nova Scotia since April 1, 2025, 15% in New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island, and 5% GST plus 9.975% QST in Quebec. Diesel is taxed on its own scale Diesel carries different per-litre rates from gasoline in most provinces: 15.45 cents against 10.87 in New Brunswick, 9.5 against 7.5 in Newfoundland and Labrador, 20.2 against 19.2 in Quebec, where the 3-cent ARTM levy applies to gasoline only. The federal excise tax on diesel is 4 cents, not 10, so its return in 2027 weighs less on a truck than on a car. Because diesel sells well above gasoline in late 2026, the sales tax on a litre of diesel is higher in cents even where the fixed tax is the same, and the overall share of tax in the price is lower. What it comes to in a few cities Because the per-litre taxes are fixed and the sales tax is a percentage, the share of tax in a litre falls when the price rises. That is why two cities with the same provincial tax can show slightly different tax shares on the same day. The table uses the price of the day where an official daily or weekly figure exists, and the estimate for tomorrow where the latest figure is a monthly average. Taxes that changed in 2025 and 2026 Several of the layers moved recently, which is why year-old breakdowns found elsewhere are wrong. The federal consumer carbon charge, which had reached 17.61 cents a litre on gasoline, was set to zero on April 1, 2025, and British Columbia eliminated its own carbon tax the same day. Nova Scotia's HST fell from 15% to 14% on April 1, 2025. Ontario made its 9-cent gasoline tax permanent on July 1, 2025. Manitoba's 2024 fuel tax holiday ended on January 1, 2025. The federal excise tax was suspended on April 20, 2026. Prince Edward Island suspended its provincial tax from September 26, 2026 to January 31, 2027, and Alberta paused its 13-cent tax from October 1, 2026 to at least December 31, 2026. What is scheduled next Two changes are already dated. Under Finance Canada's September 2026 draft legislation, the excise tax comes back at 5 cents on gasoline and 2 cents on diesel from February 1 to March 31, 2027, then at its full 10 and 4 cents on April 1, 2027. In Alberta, the quarterly rate from January 1, 2027 will be 0, 4.5, 9 or 13 cents depending on the average price of WTI oil, and it cannot rise by more than 9 cents in one quarter. The estimate on this site adds a dated change on the day it takes effect, sales tax included. Is GST or HST charged on top of the gas tax in Canada? Yes. GST, HST, and in Quebec GST plus QST, are calculated on the pump price including the provincial fuel tax, any regional levy and the federal excise tax when it applies. So a tax change of 10 cents a litre moves the price by 11.3 cents in Ontario, where HST is 13%, and by just under 11.5 cents in Quebec. Which province has the highest gas tax per litre? Among the cities this site follows, Metro Vancouver carries the highest per-litre fuel tax, 27 cents including 18.5 cents for TransLink, followed by the Montreal area, where the Quebec tax of 19.2 cents and the 3-cent ARTM levy add up to 22.2 cents. Alberta is the lowest in late 2026, with its provincial tax at zero. How much will the excise tax return add to a fill-up? With 13% HST, the full 10-cent return on April 1, 2027 adds 11.30¢/L a litre in Ontario, about $6.22 on a 55-litre fill-up. In Alberta, with GST only, it adds 10.50¢/L a litre. February and March 2027 carry half of those amounts if the draft legislation passes unchanged. Does Quebec’s carbon market add a separate tax at the pump? No separate line appears. The cost of Quebec’s cap-and-trade system, which distributors must cover, is already included in the wholesale price, as the Régie de l’énergie notes on its Montréal rack price publication. It therefore sits in the product part of the breakdown on this page, not in the tax lines.

cheapest/en.text: Today Edmonton has the lowest figure, 151.3¢/L, and Victoria the highest, 212.5¢/L. Among the 20 cities with their own official figure, regular gasoline is cheapest in Edmonton at 151.3¢/L and most expensive in Victoria at 212.5¢/L, a gap of 61.2¢/L, or $33.66 on a 55-litre fill-up. Taxes explain part of the ranking, not all of it: per-litre taxes and sales tax range from 7.2¢/L in Edmonton to 46.9¢/L in Montreal. Before taxes, the spread between the cheapest and the dearest market is still 43.1¢/L, so wholesale costs, distance from refineries and local margins weigh as much as tax rates. Figures mix sources of different dates: the Régie de l'énergie's daily survey in Quebec, Ontario's weekly survey, Atlantic regulators' maximums and, in the West, Statistics Canada monthly averages brought to tomorrow by the published estimate. Each row of the table gives its source date. The ranking Each city appears once, with its latest official figure or, where the only open source is a monthly average, the estimate for tomorrow. The two columns on the right split the price into taxes and the rest, which is what the market, the wholesalers and the stations charge. The suburbs that share a market with a larger city, such as Mississauga or Surrey, are left out of the ranking because their figure is that of the neighbouring market. Kelowna has no official average that can be reused, so it is not ranked either. Taxes or market? Of the 61.2¢/L between Edmonton and Victoria, taxes account for 22.9¢/L; the rest, 38.3¢/L, is what the product and the margins cost in each place. Before taxes, the cheapest market is Gatineau and the dearest Victoria, 43.1¢/L apart. The heaviest tax load per litre is in Montreal, the lightest in Edmonton. Two tax facts weigh on the ranking right now. In Alberta, the provincial fuel tax has not been collected since October 1, 2026, which leaves Calgary and Edmonton with little more than GST. In Metro Vancouver, the TransLink levy adds 18.5 cents a litre to the provincial tax before GST, and Victoria pays a 5.5-cent regional tax of its own. Quebec combines a higher fuel tax with two sales taxes, GST and QST, applied on top of it. The market side has its own order. Ranked before taxes, the three lowest figures today are those of Gatineau, Laval, Ottawa, and the three highest those of Victoria, Vancouver, St. John's. That order owes nothing to provincial policy: it is what remains once every tax in force on the date of each figure is taken out. Reading figures of different dates A ranking of this kind compares figures that were not all collected on the same day. Quebec's come from this morning's survey, Ontario's from the last Monday survey, the Atlantic maximums from the regulator's latest order, and the western ones from a monthly average carried forward by the estimate. When the market moves fast, a city surveyed a week ago can look cheaper or dearer than it is today. That is why the last column gives the date or the word estimate for every row, and why a difference of a cent or two between two cities should not be read as a real gap. Within Ontario Ontario has the same tax rate everywhere, so differences between its cities come from the market only. On the last weekly survey, Ottawa was the cheapest of the Ontario cities followed here at 170.8¢/L, and London, Ontario the dearest at 177.0¢/L. That gap of 6.2¢/L reflects distance from the refineries and terminals, local competition and the week of the survey, all of which move. What the gap is worth A gap per litre only matters through the litres you buy. For a driver covering 15,000 km a year at 8.5 L/100 km, about 1,275 litres, the full gap between the first and last city of the ranking is worth $780.30 a year. Few people can choose their city for fuel, but those who commute across a provincial or regional border, such as between Gatineau and Ottawa, or into Metro Vancouver from the Fraser Valley, face part of that gap every week. The gas taxes page explains each line of the tax column. Which Canadian city has the cheapest gas in 2026? On the figures of October 21, 2026, Edmonton, at 151.3¢/L for regular. The ranking changes with each survey, and western figures are estimates built from a monthly average, so a gap of a cent or two between two cities is within the error of the method rather than a real difference. Why is gas so expensive in Vancouver compared with the rest of Canada? For two reasons. Metro Vancouver pays 27 cents a litre of provincial and regional tax on regular, including 18.5 cents for TransLink, against 14.5 cents in most of British Columbia and 9 cents in Ontario. But even before taxes, the estimate for Vancouver is 174.9¢/L, against 147.4¢/L for Toronto: the West Coast market itself is dearer. Is the cheapest city the same for diesel? Not necessarily. Diesel has its own wholesale market and its own per-litre tax rates, higher than for gasoline in Quebec, New Brunswick and Newfoundland and Labrador. Switch the calculator at the top of this page to diesel to see the ranking for that fuel, built the same way and from the same sources.

toronto/en.text: Regular gasoline averaged 176.7¢/L in Toronto at the October 19, 2026 survey; the estimate for October 22, 2026 is 173.1¢/L. Toronto's official pump price comes from the Government of Ontario, which surveys self-serve stations every Monday and publishes one average for Toronto West and one for Toronto East; this page uses the mean of the two. The latest survey, dated October 19, 2026, puts regular gasoline at 176.7¢/L and diesel at 261.5¢/L, taxes included. Between two Monday surveys the price moves with the wholesale market, so the page carries the figure forward with the daily survey of the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, which follows the same New York Harbor market and is published every morning. For October 22, 2026 that gives 173.1¢/L. Replayed over 140 past weeks, this method missed the next Monday survey by 2.4¢/L on average, against 3.8¢/L for simply repeating the last price. Taxes take 16.6% of a litre: Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and the 13% HST, the federal excise tax being suspended since April 20, 2026. The official figures for Toronto Every figure below is dated and comes from a public source. The Ontario survey is weekly, so on a Thursday the newest official number is already three days old; the estimate column is what the published method expects for October 22, 2026. Premium costs 30.7¢/L more than regular at the latest survey, a spread that comes from the refinery market for higher-octane blends rather than from taxes, which are the same per litre for both grades. Diesel is priced on its own market, and with no daily open signal for it the estimate only moves when the Ontario rack price is newer than the survey. How the estimate for tomorrow is built The method starts from the Monday average, then asks what the wholesale market has done since. Ontario publishes the Toronto rack price every business day, but with about a week of delay, so on most days it stops before the survey date and cannot add anything. The Régie de l'énergie du Québec publishes its Montréal survey every morning; once its sales taxes and fuel taxes are removed, what is left moves with the same refinery and import market that supplies the Greater Toronto Area. The change in that pre-tax number since Monday, multiplied by 1.13 for HST, is added to Toronto's Monday price. It is a reasonable signal, not a forecast of what one station on Lake Shore Boulevard will post. Over the weeks replayed, its average miss was 37% smaller than that of the naive guess of "no change". The full rules, including how tax changes are dated, are on the method page . Where a Toronto litre goes At today's price the sales tax alone is 20.3¢/L. Ontario's gasoline tax has stayed at 9 cents since it was cut from 14.7 cents in July 2022, and the province made that rate permanent on July 1, 2025. The federal excise tax of 10 cents has been suspended since April 20, 2026; Finance Canada's draft legislation extends the suspension to January 31, 2027, then brings back half of it in February and March 2027 and all of it on April 1, 2027. Whatever remains after taxes pays for the gasoline itself, the pipeline and truck to the station, the wholesaler and the retailer. That share is what changes from week to week; the taxes per litre do not. The last weeks in Toronto The Ontario series is published under the Open Government Licence, so its recent surveys can be shown in full. They give a sense of how far the price travels in a quarter. What a fill-up costs A compact car with a 45-litre tank costs $79.51 to fill at the last survey price, a small SUV with 60 litres $106.02. A one-cent move changes those fill-ups by 45 and 60 cents. If you are deciding between filling up today or tomorrow, the gap between the survey and the estimate on a 55-litre fill-up is $1.98. Commuters who drive from Durham Region or Peel into the city can compare the two regional averages with the city ranking . Why does Toronto have two official gas price averages? The Government of Ontario reports the city as two markets in its weekly survey, Toronto West and Toronto East, each with its own regular, premium and diesel average. Neither is the whole city on its own, so this page takes the mean of the two on every survey date where both are published, and shows that blended figure as the Toronto price. What day of the week do Toronto gas prices change? Stations can change their posted price at any hour, and many do so overnight when their supplier changes the wholesale (rack) price. The official Ontario figure, however, is a Monday snapshot. That is why the tomorrow estimate on this page starts from Monday and adds the market movement published since, rather than pretending to know what a given station will post. Is the Toronto price the same in Mississauga and Brampton? Ontario does not publish separate averages for Mississauga or Brampton. Both sit in the Toronto West market of the provincial survey, so their pages use the Toronto West average alone, while this Toronto page blends West and East. Real station prices along Highway 401 or in Brampton can still differ by a few cents from the regional average.

mississauga/en.text: Mississauga drivers paid 176.9¢/L on average for regular at the October 19, 2026 Toronto West survey, and the estimate for October 22, 2026 is 173.3¢/L. Mississauga has no official gas price of its own: the Government of Ontario's weekly survey of self-serve stations folds the city into Toronto West, the western half of the Toronto market, so every figure on this page is the Toronto West average. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, regular gasoline there cost 176.9¢/L, premium 208.0¢/L and diesel 262.0¢/L, taxes included. Because the province only surveys on Mondays, the site carries that number forward with the wholesale movement visible since then in the daily Montreal survey of the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, sales tax added, which gives 173.3¢/L for October 22, 2026. Replayed over 140 past weeks of Toronto West, that projection was off by 2.5¢/L on average, against 3.8¢/L when the last survey is simply repeated. Tax makes up 16.6% of the litre: Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and 13% HST, while the federal excise tax stays suspended since April 20, 2026. Toronto West stands in for Mississauga The provincial survey is a Monday snapshot of self-serve prices across a handful of Ontario markets. Mississauga is not one of them by name; it falls inside Toronto West, and so do its neighbours in Peel. The table below therefore describes the western part of the Greater Toronto Area as a whole, with each figure dated and attributed. At this survey premium sat 31.1¢/L above regular and diesel 85.1¢/L above it. Those spreads come from the refined products markets, not from tax: Ontario charges the same 9 cents a litre on both gasoline grades. What a compact car costs to fill in Mississauga The simplest case is a compact car. Take a 45-litre tank bought from empty: at the survey price it costs $79.61, and at the price expected for October 22, 2026 it would cost $77.99. Each cent per litre is worth $0.45 on that fill-up, so a move of a few cents between Monday and the weekend barely changes the bill. The running cost tells a more useful story. Natural Resources Canada's median combined rating for 2026 compact models is 8.7 litres per 100 km, which puts every 100 km at $15.08 at tomorrow's estimate. Enter your posted price and how full the tank still is below. Reading tomorrow's Mississauga estimate The estimate is the Monday Toronto West average plus whatever the wholesale market has done since, measured through the daily Québec survey once its taxes are stripped out and Ontario's HST is put back. It answers one question: if the survey were taken again tomorrow, where would the average probably land? Over the weeks replayed, nine misses out of ten stayed within 5.5¢/L. It cannot say what a single forecourt on Hurontario Street or Dundas Street will post. The tomorrow page shows the same estimate for every city. Taxes inside a Mississauga litre Tax per litre is fixed in cents, then HST is charged on the whole price, so the HST part rises and falls with the pump price while the provincial tax does not. The federal excise tax of 10 cents on gasoline is at zero for now. Finance Canada's draft legislation brings back half of it on February 1, 2027 and all of it on April 1, 2027, which would add the excise plus HST on top to every litre. Recent Toronto West surveys The Ontario series is published under an open licence, so the last 13 surveys used for Mississauga can be listed in full. Drivers in the east end of the region can set these against the Toronto East figures used for Oshawa , and the national ranking places the whole market among other Canadian cities. Why does the Mississauga gas price match Toronto West exactly? The Ontario government does not publish a Mississauga average. Its weekly survey splits Greater Toronto into a western and an eastern market, and Mississauga belongs to the western one. Showing that regional figure, and saying so, is more honest than inventing a city number. A station near your home can still sit a few cents above or below it. How much does it cost to fill a compact car in Mississauga this week? With a 45-litre tank filled from empty at the Toronto West survey price of 176.9¢/L, the bill is $79.61. If some fuel is still in the tank when you stop, the calculator on this page lets you say how much remains and recomputes the litres you actually buy. Is gas in Mississauga cheaper than in central Toronto? The Toronto page blends the West and East averages, while Mississauga uses West alone. At the latest survey the blend was 176.7¢/L and Toronto West was 176.9¢/L, a gap of +0.2¢. Real stations on either side of the city limit vary more than that, so the regional gap is a rough guide only.

brampton/en.text: Regular gas in Brampton follows the Toronto West average, 176.9¢/L at the October 19, 2026 survey, with 173.3¢/L expected for October 22, 2026. Ontario does not survey Brampton on its own. The province's Monday price survey treats the city as part of Toronto West, so the figure shown here is that regional average, and it is identical to the one used for Mississauga. The survey of Monday, October 19, 2026 found regular gasoline at 176.9¢/L and diesel at 262.0¢/L, taxes in. Moving it forward with the wholesale change published since Monday gives an estimate of 173.3¢/L for October 22, 2026; on 140 replayed weeks, the method's average miss was 2.5¢/L, which beats the 3.8¢/L of a no-change guess. For a commuter the yearly bill matters more than the weekly number: at that estimate, 15,000 km in a small SUV rated at the class median burns $2,366 of fuel, a compact $2,262. Taxes are 16.7% of the price, from Ontario's 9-cent tax and the 13% HST, the federal excise being suspended since April 20, 2026. The regional figure behind Brampton Brampton's number is borrowed, and it is worth knowing from where. Each Monday the province records self-serve prices in a set of markets; Toronto West covers the western side of the Greater Toronto Area, Peel Region included. The averages below are those of that market, dated, with the estimate for October 22, 2026 beside them. The commute, counted over a year Highways 410, 401 and 407 tie Brampton to Toronto, and for anyone who drives one of them every working day a cent per litre is abstract; the yearly total is not. The table uses the median combined rating of 2026 models in each class from Natural Resources Canada and 15,000 km, which is only the calculator's starting distance. Real commutes can be much longer or shorter, and real-world consumption is often above the label. The spread between classes is the real lever. Moving from a standard SUV to a compact changes the yearly bill by $962 at today's prices, far more than any week-to-week change in the pump price. Each extra 10 cents a litre adds $137 a year to the small SUV in the example. From Monday's survey to tomorrow's number A yearly budget built on a single survey would go stale within days, which is why the calculator uses the estimate rather than the Monday figure. The site takes the Toronto West average, then adds the change in the pre-tax Montreal price published each morning by the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, grossed up by Ontario's HST. Both markets are supplied from the same eastern refining and import system, so their wholesale prices tend to move together. Diesel has no such daily signal: its estimate only shifts when Ontario's wholesale (rack) price is newer than the survey, which is why it currently reads 262.0¢/L, the same as Monday. The tomorrow page lists the estimate for every city. Brampton or Toronto for the fill-up Drivers who work downtown sometimes wonder whether to buy fuel at either end of the trip. The provincial averages do not show a large gap: Toronto West differs from the blended Toronto figure by +0.2¢ at the latest survey. The Toronto page explains how that blend is made. What the province and Ottawa take Ontario's gasoline tax is 9 cents a litre, a rate made permanent on July 1, 2025, and HST at 13% is added on top of the full price. The federal excise tax is suspended for now; its planned return in 2027 is covered on the price outlook page . The last Monday surveys Week-to-week moves in this market are visible in the published series, which is open data. How much does a year of commuting from Brampton cost in gas? It depends mostly on distance and vehicle. As an example, 15,000 km a year in a small SUV at the Natural Resources Canada class median uses about 1,365 litres, or $2,366 at tomorrow's Toronto West estimate. Change the vehicle, the distance or your own consumption rating in the calculator to get your figure. Does Brampton have its own official gas price average? No. The Government of Ontario publishes regional averages, and Brampton sits inside Toronto West, the same market as Mississauga. That is why both pages show the same number. This site states the regional source openly rather than presenting a city figure that no agency publishes. Should Brampton commuters fill up in Toronto instead? On regional averages the difference is small: the Toronto figure, which blends West and East, was 176.7¢/L at the latest survey, against 176.9¢/L for Toronto West. On a 55-litre fill-up that is $0.11. Detouring for it rarely pays; a cheaper station on your usual route matters more.

oshawa/en.text: Oshawa takes the Toronto East average, 176.5¢/L for regular at the October 19, 2026 survey, and 172.9¢/L is the estimate for October 22, 2026. The Government of Ontario does not publish an Oshawa average. Its weekly survey splits the Greater Toronto Area into two markets, and Durham Region falls into Toronto East, so the figures here are that market's. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, regular gasoline averaged 176.5¢/L and diesel 261.0¢/L with all taxes. On the same date Toronto West, the market used for Mississauga and Brampton, was at 176.9¢/L: Toronto East was cheaper by 0.4¢/L. The site's estimate for October 22, 2026 is 172.9¢/L, built from Monday's survey and the wholesale change that the daily Québec survey has shown since; tried on 140 past weeks, it missed the next survey by 2.4¢/L on average, compared with 3.8¢/L for carrying the old price. Tax is 16.6% of each litre, made of Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and 13% HST; the federal excise has been suspended since April 20, 2026. Durham Region in the provincial survey The province publishes averages for markets, not for municipalities. For the area around Lake Ontario's north shore east of the city, from Pickering out to Oshawa, the relevant market is Toronto East. Every figure in this table belongs to it and is dated by the survey that produced it. Toronto East against Toronto West Because the Toronto page blends the two halves of the region, the comparison between them gets lost there. Here it is laid out on its own. On the latest survey, Toronto East was cheaper by 0.4¢/L. For diesel the two markets stood at 261.0¢/L and 262.0¢/L. Across those 13 weeks the East was the cheaper side 10 times and the West 3 times. The average difference, −0.5¢ for the East, is smaller than the method’s own typical error on a single week, which says something useful: the two halves of the region move almost in step, and the data files tie both to the same Toronto wholesale (rack) price. Within one market, the station you pick can matter as much as the regional average. The estimate for October 22, 2026 Ontario surveys on Monday and publishes once. To fill the days between, the site takes the pre-tax change in the Montreal market reported each morning by the Régie de l'énergie du Québec and adds it, HST included, to the Toronto East average. Nine weeks in ten during the replay, the miss stayed under 5.2¢/L. The rules are described on the method page . The tax in an Oshawa litre Ontario taxes gasoline at 9 cents a litre and adds 13% HST to the full price, so at the Toronto East average the HST alone is 20.3¢/L. That HST share is the only tax that moves with the market; the per-litre taxes are set in cents and stay put whatever the price does. The tax page compares this with the other provinces. One change is already on the calendar. The federal excise tax, 10 cents a litre on gasoline before its suspension on April 20, 2026, is due back at half rate on February 1, 2027 and in full on April 1, 2027 under Finance Canada's draft legislation. With HST charged on top, a driver in Durham buying a full tank every week would feel it at every fill-up; the calculator below turns it into a monthly figure. The Toronto East series The weekly series is published under the Open Government Licence of Ontario, which is why the full list can be reproduced here. Which official gas price applies to Oshawa? The Toronto East average from the Government of Ontario's Monday survey of self-serve stations. Oshawa and the rest of Durham Region are not surveyed separately, so this page uses the eastern half of the Toronto market and says so in every table. Individual stations in Oshawa, Whitby or Ajax can post prices a little above or below that average. Is gas usually cheaper in Oshawa than in Mississauga? Over the 13 recent surveys published for both markets, Toronto East came in cheaper 10 times and Toronto West 3 times, with an average gap of −0.5¢ for the East. The gap is small and changes sign, so it is not a reason to plan a trip across the region for fuel. Why is Oshawa diesel priced so far above regular gasoline? At the latest survey diesel in Toronto East was 261.0¢/L, which is 84.5¢/L above regular. Taxes do not explain it: Ontario charges 9 cents a litre on both fuels. The difference comes from the distillate market, which has its own supply and demand, and it is passed on with HST at the pump.

hamilton/en.text: For Hamilton the reference is the southern Ontario average, which put regular at 175.2¢/L on October 19, 2026; the estimate for October 22, 2026 is 171.6¢/L. Hamilton is not one of the markets in the Government of Ontario's weekly fuel price survey, so there is no official Hamilton average to quote. The closest published figure is the southern Ontario average, a single number that the province computes across the southern part of Ontario every Monday, and this page uses it. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, it was 175.2¢/L for regular, 205.5¢/L for premium and 261.6¢/L for diesel, taxes included. The nearest surveyed city, St. Catharines and Niagara, has its own series: on that date St. Catharines and Niagara was 0.8¢/L below it. The estimate for October 22, 2026, 171.6¢/L, adds the wholesale change seen since Monday in the daily Montreal survey; over 140 replayed weeks it was off by 2.3¢/L on average, a no-change guess by 3.7¢/L. Taxes, 9 cents of Ontario gasoline tax plus 13% HST with the federal excise suspended since April 20, 2026, are 16.6% of the price. A regional average, not a city one The Ontario survey reports averages for a short list of markets (Toronto West and East, Ottawa, London, Windsor, St. Catharines, Peterborough and several northern cities) along with a provincial, a southern and a northern average. Hamilton is not on the list. The southern average is the published number that covers it, so it is the one used here. It blends many places, which smooths out local quirks: a Hamilton station can be cheaper or dearer than this figure on any given week. Premium was 30.3¢/L above regular in the survey, diesel 86.4¢/L above. Those gaps are set by the refined products markets; the provincial tax per litre is the same on both grades of gasoline. Hamilton against St. Catharines and Niagara St. Catharines, a short drive along the Queen Elizabeth Way, is the closest market the province surveys by name. Its average can be set beside the southern Ontario average for each week where both were published. In 13 of those 13 weeks Niagara came in below the southern average, and the mean difference was −1.9¢. Keep in mind what is being compared: one side is a single urban market, the other an average of the whole south of the province, so a gap may say as much about the rest of southern Ontario as about either city. The full Niagara picture is on the St. Catharines page . How the Hamilton estimate moves The southern average is a Monday number. Between surveys, the site follows the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, which publishes a Montreal price every morning; with its taxes removed, its change since Monday is a fair read of where the eastern wholesale market went, and it is applied to the southern average with HST. In the replay, nine weeks out of ten the error stayed below 5.4¢/L. The tomorrow page gives the same estimate for all cities. Taxes per litre in Hamilton Hamilton drivers pay the same taxes as everywhere else in Ontario: 9 cents a litre of provincial gasoline tax and 13% HST. No regional fuel tax is added on top, unlike the transit levies charged in Metro Vancouver or around Montreal. On a 55-litre fill-up at this price, $16.04 goes to taxes and $80.32 to the fuel itself, its transport and the margins of the wholesaler and the retailer. Recent southern Ontario surveys For a national view, the city ranking lines up every surveyed market from the cheapest to the most expensive. Why does this page use the southern Ontario average for Hamilton? Because the province publishes nothing narrower for the city. Its weekly survey reports a handful of markets by name and two broad averages, one for the south of the province and one for the north. Hamilton falls in the southern one. Using it, and saying so, avoids presenting a city figure that no public agency produces. Is gas cheaper in Hamilton or in St. Catharines? The two cannot be compared station by station from public data, only through their averages. Over the 13 recent surveys, the St. Catharines and Niagara figure was below the southern Ontario average 13 times, with an average difference of −1.9¢. That is a comparison of a regional average with a city average, not of two cities on equal terms. How much does a fill-up cost in Hamilton at the moment? With the southern Ontario average at 175.2¢/L, 55 litres of regular cost $96.36 and 65 litres $113.88. The fill-up calculator on the page lets you enter the price on the sign instead, which is the better figure when you are standing at the pump.

kitchener/en.text: In Kitchener-Waterloo diesel stood at 261.6¢/L and regular at 175.2¢/L on the October 19, 2026 southern Ontario average. Kitchener-Waterloo is not surveyed by name in the Government of Ontario's weekly fuel price report, so the official figure that applies to it is the southern Ontario average. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, that average put diesel at 261.6¢/L and regular gasoline at 175.2¢/L, a gap of 86.4¢/L, taxes included. Regular is expected at 171.6¢/L on October 22, 2026 once the wholesale move since Monday is added; diesel has no daily public signal, so its estimate stays at 261.6¢/L until the provincial rack price catches up. Replayed over 140 weeks, the diesel method missed by 4.3¢/L on average and the gasoline one by 2.3¢/L. For a standard SUV driven 20,000 km, the class medians from Natural Resources Canada give $4,256 a year on gasoline and $5,441 on diesel at those prices. Taxes take 14.9% of a litre of diesel: Ontario's 9 cents plus 13% HST, with the federal excise of 4 cents suspended since April 20, 2026. Kitchener-Waterloo in the Ontario survey The provincial survey names a few markets and then gives broader averages. Kitchener-Waterloo is in the broad one for the south of the province, the southern Ontario average, and every number below comes from it, with its date and its source. The two fuels are estimated in different ways. Regular gasoline is carried from Monday to October 22, 2026 with the daily Montreal survey of the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, whose pre-tax change tracks the wholesale market that also supplies southern Ontario; in the replay its miss stayed under 5.4¢/L nine weeks out of ten. The daily Québec survey covers regular gasoline only, so for diesel the site waits for Ontario's rack series, which lags by about a week. That is why the diesel column often shows no change, and why its past error, 4.3¢/L on average, is wider than the gasoline one. The tomorrow page gives both for every city. Diesel in Kitchener-Waterloo Diesel is priced off a different refinery stream than gasoline, middle distillates rather than light products, and in this survey it is 86.4¢/L above regular. Tax is not the reason. Ontario's fuel tax is 9 cents a litre on both, and the federal excise, when it applies, is lower on diesel, 4 cents against 10. The breakdown of a litre of diesel at the survey price shows where the money goes. Compared with a litre of regular, which carries 20.2¢/L of HST, a litre of diesel carries 30.1¢/L, simply because HST is a percentage of a higher price. The diesel page explains the separate market and how its estimate is built for every city. A standard SUV on gasoline or on diesel In the 2026 ratings, diesel versions are listed for 8 standard SUVs and 8 full-size pickups. Natural Resources Canada's 2026 ratings give a median combined consumption of 12.4 L/100 km for standard SUVs on gasoline and 10.4 L/100 km for the 8 diesel ones. Using the estimates for October 22, 2026 and 20,000 km a year, a round example distance: The fuel saving of a diesel engine is real, but in Ontario right now it is not enough to offset the higher price at the pump. The break-even sits at about 204.6¢/L for diesel with regular at its current estimate; below that line the diesel SUV is cheaper per kilometre, above it the gasoline one is. That comparison covers fuel only; purchase price, maintenance and resale value are left out. When the diesel excise comes back Finance Canada's draft legislation restores the federal excise on diesel at 2 cents on February 1, 2027 and 4 cents on April 1, 2027, against 5 and 10 cents for gasoline. With HST on top, the return weighs less on a diesel driver per litre. Recent surveys for Kitchener-Waterloo The same southern average serves Hamilton ; London , further west on Highway 401, has its own surveyed market. What is the diesel price in Kitchener-Waterloo this week? The latest official figure is 261.6¢/L, the southern Ontario average for diesel at the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026. The province does not survey Kitchener-Waterloo on its own, so this is the regional average. A given station in Kitchener, Waterloo or Cambridge can sit several cents away from it, so the price on the sign is what to enter in the fill-up calculator. Is a diesel SUV cheaper to run than a gasoline one in Kitchener? At current prices, no: over 20,000 km the diesel class median costs $5,441 a year against $4,256 for gasoline. The answer turns on the price gap. Diesel wins only while it stays below about 204.6¢/L with regular at today's estimate, and only 8 standard SUV models in the 2026 ratings run on diesel. Why does the Kitchener diesel estimate not change from Monday? The gasoline estimate moves with the daily Montreal survey, which only covers regular gasoline. For diesel the site can only use Ontario's wholesale (rack) price, published with about a week of delay. When that series has nothing newer than the Monday survey, the honest estimate is the survey itself, which is what the page shows.

barrie/en.text: Barrie's reference price, the southern Ontario average, was 175.2¢/L for regular on October 19, 2026, with 171.6¢/L estimated for October 22, 2026. There is no official Barrie gas price: the Government of Ontario's Monday survey of self-serve stations does not list the city, and the published figure that covers it is the southern Ontario average. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, it stood at 175.2¢/L for regular and 205.5¢/L for premium, taxes included, which is 1.5¢/L below the blended Toronto figure on the same day. For October 22, 2026 the estimate is 171.6¢/L, obtained by adding to Monday's average the wholesale change since then in the Régie de l'énergie du Québec's daily Montreal survey; over 140 replayed weeks its average error was 2.3¢/L, where a no-change guess erred by 3.7¢/L. For a driver who fills a 65-litre tank once a week, that price comes to about $483 a month. Taxes are 16.6% of the pump price (Ontario's 9 cents and 13% HST), and the federal excise suspended since April 20, 2026 is due back in 2027. Where Barrie's figure comes from Barrie sits on Highway 400 north of Toronto, at the edge of Lake Simcoe, outside both of the Toronto markets in the provincial survey. The province publishes the southern Ontario average every Monday, and that is the number that applies here. It is an average of a wide area, so local stations can be cheaper or more expensive than it in a given week. A Highway 400 commute in a monthly budget For a driver who heads down the 400 to the Greater Toronto Area several times a week, the useful unit is the month. Take one 65-litre fill-up a week as a simple example. That is about 282 litres a month, which at the estimate for October 22, 2026 comes to $483. Each cent per litre moves that monthly bill by $2.82, and over the last 13 surveys the average ranged across 24.5¢/L, which on this budget is a difference of $69 a month between the cheapest and the dearest week. A budget built this way is easier to hold to than a price watch. Knowing that the commute costs roughly a fixed amount a month, and how much a ten-cent move shifts it, tells you whether a cheaper station on the way is worth the stop. Enter your own vehicle and yearly kilometres below; the result also gives the cost per 100 km. Barrie against Toronto Commuters can fill up at either end of the trip. The published averages put the southern Ontario figure 1.5¢/L below the Toronto blend at the latest survey. On a 65-litre fill-up that is $0.98, rarely worth a detour. The 2027 excise in the commuter's budget The federal excise tax on gasoline, 10 cents a litre, has been suspended since April 20, 2026. Finance Canada's draft legislation extends the suspension to January 31, 2027, brings back 5 cents on February 1, 2027 and the full 10 cents on April 1, 2027. HST is charged on top of it, so in Barrie the return is worth 5.65¢/L and then 11.30¢/L if nothing else moves. For the weekly fill-up in the example, that adds $32 a month from April 2027. The outlook page follows the schedule. Taxes in a Barrie litre today Until then, a litre of regular in Barrie carries Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and HST at 13% on the whole price, nothing more. The excise line reads zero for as long as the suspension lasts. The last southern Ontario surveys Hamilton and Kitchener-Waterloo share this average; the ranking shows where it falls among Canadian cities. Is gas cheaper in Barrie than in Toronto? On the published averages the difference is small. The southern Ontario figure used for Barrie was 175.2¢/L at the latest survey and the Toronto blend 176.7¢/L, so the Barrie figure was 1.5¢/L below Toronto's. That compares a regional average with a city one, so treat it as a rough guide rather than a rule for where to fill up. How much does a weekly Highway 400 commute from Barrie cost in fuel? It depends on your distance and vehicle, so the page gives an example: one 65-litre fill-up a week is about 282 litres a month, or $483 at tomorrow's estimate. The calculator lets you replace that with your own kilometres and consumption to get a yearly and monthly figure. How will the 2027 excise tax change gas prices in Barrie? Under Finance Canada's draft legislation the federal excise on gasoline returns at 5 cents on February 1, 2027 and 10 cents on April 1, 2027. With 13% HST charged on top, that is +5.65¢ and then +11.30¢ a litre in Barrie, all else being equal, or $32 a month for the weekly fill-up in the example.

ottawa/en.text: Ottawa's regular gasoline averaged 170.8¢/L at the October 19, 2026 Ontario survey, and the estimate for October 22, 2026 is 167.2¢/L. Ottawa is one of the markets that the Government of Ontario surveys by name every Monday, so the city has its own official average. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026 it was 170.8¢/L for regular and 264.1¢/L for diesel, taxes included; Statistics Canada's monthly average for September 2026, a separate survey, was 178.4¢/L. The estimate for October 22, 2026 is 167.2¢/L: Monday's figure plus the pre-tax change since then in the daily Montreal survey of the Régie de l'énergie du Québec, with HST. Over 140 replayed weeks it missed the next survey by 2.5¢/L on average, against 3.8¢/L for a no-change guess. Across the Ottawa River, the Régie's daily average for Gatineau on October 21, 2026 was 175.3¢/L. Taxes make up 16.8% of an Ottawa litre, from Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and 13% HST; the federal excise has been suspended since April 20, 2026. Ottawa's own weekly average Unlike the suburbs of Toronto, Ottawa has a market of its own in the provincial survey, so the figures below describe the city rather than a wider region. They are dated by the Monday survey that produced them. Statistics Canada also publishes an Ottawa average, monthly, in table 18-10-0001-01. For September 2026 it was 178.4¢/L. That is +7.6¢ from the latest Ontario survey, but the two series are collected differently and cover different periods, a full month on one side and a single Monday on the other; the weekly Ontario survey is the fresher of the two and is the one the estimate starts from. Ottawa and Gatineau, either side of the river Gatineau faces Ottawa across the Ottawa River, and several bridges link the two. The two cities sit in different tax systems and are measured by different agencies: Ontario's weekly survey for Ottawa, the Régie de l'énergie du Québec's daily survey for Gatineau. On the most recent dates available, Gatineau was at 175.3¢/L on October 21, 2026, and Ottawa is estimated at 167.2¢/L for October 22, 2026, a gap of +8.1¢ for Gatineau. The tax side explains part of the picture. Quebec's fuel tax is 19.2 cents a litre, but within 15 km of the Ontario border it is reduced by 6 cents, which brings Gatineau to 13.2 cents against Ontario's 9. Quebec then charges GST and QST together at 14.975%, against 13% HST in Ontario. All told, taxes come to 36.0¢/L in Gatineau at its price and 28.6¢/L in Ottawa at the survey price. Whatever remains of the gap comes from wholesale supply and retail competition on each side. The Gatineau page gives the Quebec side in detail, and Montreal shows the effect of the transit levy charged there. Ottawa among Ontario markets Of the 5 Ontario cities on this site that have a surveyed market of their own (Toronto counted once, as the mean of its two halves), Ottawa was the cheapest at the latest survey. Cities that borrow a regional figure, such as Mississauga or Hamilton, are left out of the ranking so that no average is counted twice. The tax inside an Ottawa litre The provincial rate of 9 cents was cut from 14.7 cents in July 2022 and made permanent in 2025. The tax page sets it beside every other province. Recent Ottawa surveys The province publishes its weekly series under an open licence, so the recent Ottawa surveys can be shown in full. They show how far the price can travel within a few months, and how much of that movement a single week can hold. The estimate for the coming days is explained on the tomorrow page . Is gas cheaper in Ottawa or in Gatineau? On the latest figures, Gatineau's daily average of 175.3¢/L (October 21, 2026) is +8.1¢ from the Ottawa estimate for October 22, 2026, 167.2¢/L. Quebec taxes are heavier, but Quebec cuts its fuel tax by 6 cents within 15 km of Ontario, which narrows the gap. Compare the two sources on dates as close as possible. Why are there two official gas prices for Ottawa? Two agencies measure it. The Government of Ontario surveys self-serve stations every Monday; Statistics Canada publishes a monthly average in its consumer price data. They differ in method and period, so they rarely match to the cent. This page leads with the Ontario survey because it is weekly and recent, and keeps the monthly figure as a cross-check. Where does Ottawa rank among Ontario cities for gas prices? At the latest survey Ottawa was the cheapest of the 5 Ontario cities on this site with a surveyed market of their own, at 170.8¢/L. The ranking can change from one Monday to the next, so the city ranking page recomputes it with every update of the data.

london/en.text: Regular gasoline in London averaged 177.0¢/L at the October 19, 2026 survey and is estimated at 173.4¢/L for October 22, 2026. London is surveyed as its own market by the Government of Ontario, which records self-serve prices there every Monday for three fuels. At the survey of Monday, October 19, 2026, regular gasoline averaged 177.0¢/L, premium 207.6¢/L and diesel 259.8¢/L, taxes included, so premium cost 30.6¢/L more than regular. Since the province publishes only once a week, the site moves Monday's figure forward with the pre-tax change in the Montreal survey that the Régie de l'énergie du Québec posts every morning, and adds HST; for October 22, 2026 that gives 173.4¢/L for regular. Replayed on 140 past weeks of the London series, the estimate missed the next survey by 2.5¢/L on average, while repeating the old price missed by 3.8¢/L. Out of a litre of regular, 16.6% is tax, from Ontario's 9-cent gasoline tax and the 13% HST, the federal excise being suspended since April 20, 2026. London's weekly survey London appears under its own name in the provincial survey, so the figures below describe the city's stations rather than a regional mix. Each line gives the survey date, the estimate the method expects for October 22, 2026 and the size of its past errors. Premium or regular in London The price gap between grades in London was 30.6¢/L at the latest survey. Very little of that is tax: the Ontario gasoline tax is 9 cents a litre on both grades, so only the HST, charged as a percentage, grows with the higher price. At the survey prices a litre of premium carries 23.9¢/L of HST against 20.4¢/L for regular. The rest of the gap is set in the refinery market for high-octane blending components. Over a year the difference becomes visible. With a mid-size car at the Natural Resources Canada class median of 8.3 L/100 km and 15,000 km, a round example, choosing premium costs $381 more. The owner's manual states whether the engine requires premium or only recommends it, which is the question to settle before paying the gap. Try your own numbers on a fill-up below. Along Highway 401 London lies on Highway 401 between Windsor and Toronto , with Kitchener-Waterloo on the way east.
